title: Chapter 182 – The Night of Counting
html:
[The Garden Hall, Roll Room – Zhao]

The tide goes out on the seventh morning, and Zhao stands on the Hall steps and watches it leave like a tenant who has stayed too long.

There is no horn. There is no drum. There is only the slow gray light climbing the eastern ridge, and the smell of wet ash, and the sound of a great many small things moving away. The crawlers go first, in long pale ribbons, drifting down the lower terraces toward the river. The Gnashers follow at a heavy walk, heads low. A few stragglers linger in the orchard, snuffling at the burned stumps, and then they too wander off. By the second hour the Garden is empty of them, as a beach is empty after the sea has drawn back, leaving wreckage.

She does not cheer. Nobody does. They stand along the Hall's long terrace in their hundreds, farmers and cooks and scribes and children, wrapped in blankets, red-eyed, filthy, and watch the valley come back to them.

It is wrecked. The orchard is a churned black field. The lower terraces are gone. The observatory on the east ridge, Ning Ruiyan's pride, is a heap of broken stone with a single brass ring still gleaming on the top of it, like a coin dropped in a ditch. Smoke rises from forty places. A dead Gnasher lies across the main road like a felled tree.

"Mistress," says a quiet voice at her shoulder.

It is Pei An, with the Roll under his arm.

He is seventy-nine, and he looks a hundred. The clerk's bent back has bent further. His beard has gone from gray to white in a week. But his hands, long, inky, spotted with age, hold the great leather volume as tenderly as a mother holds a child, and his eyes behind their cracked spectacles are bright.

"It is time," he says.

"I know."

"Shall I begin the counting?"

"Not yet." Zhao closes her eyes. "Let them have one hour of it. One hour of looking at the sun."

Pei An bows. "As you say, Clan Head."

She stands for the hour. And when it is over, she turns to the door, and the long hall behind it, and the work she has put off for seven days.

* * *

Tian Mo gives his report on the terrace, standing, because he will not sit.

He has come up the long stair for the first time in a week. His left sleeve hangs empty and pinned. His face is hollow, and a fresh scar runs from his hairline to the point of his jaw, and he leans on a plain staff held in his right hand. Behind him, in a ragged line, stand the guards of the fifth landing: forty-one men and women. There were forty-three.

"The Dock is secure," he says. "The Pebble is cracked, but Yue says it is bound. The stair is clean. The roots have drawn back. I have posted sentries at the foot of the shaft and at the Gate, and at each landing."

"Casualties?"

"Two of mine. Pol, who took the leg wound on the first night, and a woman named Reyes. Both of them died in the cellar infirmary." He pauses. "Dai is whole. The stone creature has lost a hand and refuses to be repaired. Lin Kuang says it looks better that way."

"And you?"

"I am alive."

"That is not what I asked."

He looks at her. His eyes, which she has always thought were the plainest eyes in the Garden, are deep and tired and clear. "I am missing an arm," he says. "I am a one-armed Warden of a stair that nobody will climb again for a generation. I am thirty-four years old, and I think I have just discovered what I am for." He bows, a short stiff bow. "I would like to keep the stair, if the clan will have me."

"You will keep it," says Zhao.

"With one arm."

"With one arm, or none." She almost smiles. "Warden, you held a landing against a Rider with a hole in your side. I do not think the clan will quarrel about the number of your hands."

He nods. He does not trust himself to speak. He goes back down the terrace at his slow even stride, and his guards fall in behind him, and she watches them go.

Forty-one, she thinks. And the stair.

She does not yet know the figure for the whole clan. She knows only that it is large.

* * *

The counting is the oldest custom of the Lin clan, older than the Garden, older than the name.

It goes back to the first Patriarch, who led thirty families out of a burning city on foot, and who stood on the far bank of a river with a notched stick, making a notch for each person who had crossed. He had no paper. He had no ink. He had a stick, and a habit of being honest, and when the last of them was across, he counted the notches, and the number was less than he had started with. So he sat down on the bank and said their names aloud, one by one, until there was no one left to name.

That is the Night of Counting. It is not a ceremony. It is a duty. After every great loss, the Clan Head sits with the Roll through the dark, and reads the names, the living and the dead, aloud, in order, to anyone who comes to listen. The dead are struck from the active column and entered in the black. The living are marked present. No one may skip a name. No one may be forgotten.

She has done it twice before. Once after the plague, when she was forty. Once after the fire that took the east wing, when she was sixty. Both times it took her all night, and both times she was left, at dawn, with a hollow in her chest the size of a child.

This one will take longer.

The Roll Room is a long low chamber behind the Hall, lined with shelves of ledgers, lit by a single oil-lamp on a high desk. It smells of ink and dust. At one end is the Clan Head's chair, a plain straight-backed thing of black oak. At the other is the door. Between them, on the floor, sit the living: a hundred, two hundred, three, wrapped in blankets and silence, waiting.

Zhao sits down. Pei An lays the Roll on the desk and opens it. The pages are cream-colored, soft with handling, ruled in faint blue, and each line holds a name in his small neat hand.

"Begin," she says.

* * *

She has reached the Ls when her husband's cot is carried into the room.

She sees it from the corner of her eye: four guards, bearing it gently on their shoulders, a blanket draped across. They set it down at the foot of her chair. They bow. They go.

Dao lies under the blanket with his eyes open.

He has been dying for a month. She has known it the way she knows the weather, in the joints. The cough began in autumn and did not stop. He grew thin, then thinner. He stopped eating the festival wine, and then stopped eating at all. The healers shook their heads. Bell, the only honest one, told her plainly: His heart is tired. He is eighty-four. He may have weeks.

It has been three.

"Zhao," he says. His voice is a thread.

"Don't talk."

"I want to listen." The old square face creases. It was a good face once, broad and brown and wide-mouthed, a face for laughing. Now the bones stand out, and the eyes are huge, but they are still his eyes, still twinkling. "You're reading the Roll. I always liked it. You do the voices."

"I do not do voices."

"You do. When you read Old Hu's name, you go gruff. When you read Pei An's, you go prim." He smiles. "Go on."

She does not trust her own voice. But she takes the next page, and reads, steadily, in the flat clear tone of her office, and a hundred faces turn toward her. She reads the names of the living, and a murmur of present ripples back from the audience. She reads the names of the dead, in the cold slow cadence the custom requires, and each time a name falls, someone in the dark gives a small choked cry.

She does the voices. She cannot help it. It is the only way she has ever been able to say them.

"Read me the Ds," Dao murmurs, between pages.

"The Ds are not till later."

"Humor me."

She flips back. There are only a few in the active column: Dai, the guard; Dun, with his new daughter; Du Mei-lin, who runs the dye-sheds. She reads them, and Dao nods with his eyes shut.

"Is mine in there?"

"Yours is under L, you old fool. Lin Dao."

"Is it in the black column yet?"

"No."

"Well." The dry whisper of a laugh. "Do me a kindness. Leave it a while. I would like to sit in the active column a little longer, if it's all the same. It's very comfortable."

She cannot answer. She turns the page.

"Zhao," he says.

"I am reading."

"You were right about the lamps." His fingers tighten on hers. "I heard. Qinghe talked you out of the dark. I never did think much of the dark. It's no good for soup."

"Be quiet."

"I'm only saying. You were wise to listen."

"I am eighty-two years old," says Zhao, in a rough voice. "I have been wise to listen to the cook for sixty. It is the only secret of ruling."

He laughs. It is the last time she hears it, though she does not know that yet.

Dao lies and listens with his eyes closed. At the hundredth name, he takes her hand.

* * *

At the tenth hour, the door opens, and a girl comes in with a baby.

She is perhaps seventeen, with a plaster over one eye, and she stands in the doorway uncertainly, clutching a bundle of cloth. A hush falls. Zhao lifts her head. The girl bobs a clumsy bow and says, in a very small voice, "I was told to come here. To be counted. Is that right?"

"Come in," says Zhao. "What is your name?"

"Sun. Sun of the lower orchard."

Pei An's pen scratches. "I have a Sun of the lower orchard, Mistress. Listed as missing."

"She is not missing," says Zhao. "She is here."

The girl comes forward. She lays the bundle on the corner of the desk, and the cloth falls open, and a baby with a fist in its mouth looks up at the lamp with large solemn eyes. "He's four months," she says. "I don't know his mother. She was a pear-picker. She died in the cellar, I think. I couldn't leave him." Her voice cracks. "A man helped us. An old man with a staff. He told us to keep warm and wait for the horn."

Zhao's heart gives a strange slow lurch.

"What did he look like?"

"Gray. Thin. He coughed blood. He gave the guard a black pill." Sun swallows. "He carried the baby down to the cellar himself. He said the baby should be kept warm."

Zhao looks at Qinghe at the back of the room. Qinghe has put down the kettle.

"He did," Zhao says gently. "That sounds like him."

"Is he... is he all right?"

"No," says Zhao. "But he is doing what he can."

She turns to Pei An. "Enter the child. Under my name, and Dao's. A foundling of the Lin clan. Give him the name the girl chooses."

Sun stares. "I can choose?"

"You carried him eleven miles through a tide. I think you have the right."

The girl looks down at the baby for a long time. When she speaks, it is in a whisper. "Jian," she says. "Is that all right? After the old man?"

Zhao closes her eyes.

"That," she says, "is a very good name."

* * *

Jian himself comes in at the eleventh hour, late and silent, and sits on the floor by the door.

She does not remark on it. She sees him from the corner of her eye, a thin gray figure with a staff across his knees, hunched between a pillar and a shelf of old ledgers. He has the look of a man who has been a long way down and has not entirely come up. A pale seam of silver runs through his hair at the temple that was not there a day ago. His eyes, when she meets them across the room, are strangely clear.

He listens to the whole of the next hour without moving.

At the end of the M's, when Pei An pauses to blot, he stands and crosses the floor to where Qinghe sits with the kettle. He bends. He says something in her ear. Zhao cannot hear it, but she sees Qinghe's face change: a long still moment, and then a short astonished huff of a laugh, wet and helpless, that she covers with her hand.

"What did he say?" asks Zhao afterward.

"That Lan Wen sent a message." Qinghe's eyes are bright. "She said my tea was never as bad as she told me."

"Was it?"

"It was terrible," says Qinghe, and laughs again, and wipes her face on her smock. "Every cup. I knew it. She knew I knew."

"Then why say it?"

"I think," says Qinghe slowly, "because she wanted me to keep brewing."

* * *

Ning Ruiyan finds her in the corridor outside the Roll Room, at the turn of the night, with soot on her face and a brass ring in her hands.

She is forty-one, a lean, sharp-featured woman in a scorched blue gown, who has spent half her life on the east ridge counting the stars and the other half arguing about the count. She holds the ring against her chest as one holds an infant. It is the size of a dinner plate, dented, blackened, its fine engraved scales half melted.

"It was all that was left," she says. "I dug it out myself. I thought you should see."

"It is a fine ring."

"It is the lens-mount. The lens is gone. The tower is gone. The three hundred volumes of observations are gone, forty years of my teacher's work and my own." Her voice is a dry rasp. "And I stood on the ridge and watched it fall, Zhao, and the only thing I could think was, I hope the clerk has a copy of the index."

"He does."

"Of course he does." A bitter little laugh. "He has a copy of everything."

Zhao puts her hand over the ring, over the other woman's cold fingers. "You will build another."

"With what?"

"With what we have." She holds Ning's eyes. "The clan is not a pile of stones. It is a habit of getting up in the morning. We have done it before. We will do it again, and you will have a new tower, and your pupils will count new stars."

Ning looks at her a long moment.

"You have changed," she says, at last.

"I have lost a great deal."

"No. I mean you have stopped trying to be hard." The astronomer bends and kisses her cheek, quickly, roughly. "I like it better."

She goes away down the corridor with the ring held to her chest, and Zhao stands a moment and touches the place on her cheek.

* * *

By the twelfth hour, Pei An hands her the tally.

It is a single sheet, folded in thirds, in his small neat hand. She reads it standing at the desk, in the lamplight, with the whole room watching. Living, 961. Dead, 143. Missing, 0. Below that, a line in smaller script: Clan strength at the start of the siege, 1,104.

She reads it three times. She folds it again.

"One hundred and forty-three," she says aloud.

A silence.

"It is less than I feared," she says. "It is more than I can bear." She lifts her eyes to the room. "Hear me. Every name I have read tonight is a person who stood between you and the dark. They stood with their hands and their backs and their last breath. We will not forget them. We will write them in the black, and we will say them every year at the Night of Counting, until the Garden falls into the sea."

No one answers. But a hundred heads bow.

"And the living?" says Pei An, softly. "Do you wish to say something to the living?"

She thinks about it.

"Eat," she says. "And sleep. And tomorrow, begin again."

It is not much of a speech. But she sees Qinghe nod, and Feng wipe his nose on his sleeve, and Bell, in the doorway, let out a long shaky breath. It is enough.

* * *

At midnight, Pei An puts down his pen.

He does it very carefully, with a small click, as though afraid of breaking something. He has been recording the black column all night, writing each name as she reads it in the thin fine hand of forty years, and she has not looked at him. Now she does. He is sitting at his high desk with his hands folded and his face gray and calm.

"Pei An?"

"I am here, Mistress."

"You look unwell."

"I am seventy-nine." The faintest twinkle. "Everyone looks unwell at seventy-nine."

"You should rest."

"After the count." He lifts his chin. "I have been keeping this Roll for forty-one years. I have written every birth in this clan, and every death. I have made mistakes. I have crossed out names I should not have, and added names I should not. I have never once failed to finish a count." He looks at the book. "I would like to finish this one."

She watches him. And she understands, with a slow cold clarity, that he knows.

"How long?" she says.

"A little while. An hour, perhaps." He says it calmly. "It began in the third hour. A tightness in the arm. The healer says it is the heart." A thin smile. "The Roll Room is not a bad place to stop."

"Pei An—"

"It is all right, Clan Head. I have made my peace." He turns a page. "I have only one request."

"Anything."

"The last name." He picks up the pen. "When we reach the end, I should like to write it myself."

She does not ask whose. She nods.

The reading goes on. Pei An writes. He writes with a steady hand through the L's and the M's and the long row of Zhaos, and the audience in the dark grows hushed, because they have seen. Qinghe is there, at the back, with the black kettle, standing as straight as a spear. Feng sits beside her, his drumsticks forgotten in his lap. Bell has come in from the infirmary and stands in the doorway with her arms wrapped around her ribs.

At the end of the Ws, Pei An puts the pen down again.

"Mistress," he says, quite softly. "I believe it is my turn."

* * *

He dies at his desk, between one line and the next.

He has just finished the last name. It is not Dao. She had braced for Dao. It is a girl of nine, a Garden child named Ping, who was caught in the lower corridor on the fourth night and carried out of the cellars under a blanket. Pei An writes it with great care. He blots it. He looks at it a long moment, and says, "Ping. Daughter of Hu. Aged nine." And then, in an entirely ordinary voice, he says, "I think that is everyone."

"Yes," says Zhao.

"Good. That is good." He closes the Roll. He lays both hands on the cover, one on top of the other, the way a man lays his hands on the head of a sleeping dog. "It is a fine book."

"It is."

"I should have liked to see the next volume."

"You will," says Zhao. "I will see to it."

His eyes close. His chin drops to his chest, gently. And that is all. There is no sound, no struggle, no cry. The clerk of the Lin clan sits at his high desk with his spectacles askew and a smear of ink on his cuff, and is gone.

For a long time nobody moves. Then Qinghe puts down the kettle, and crosses the floor, and kneels in front of him. She touches his hand, and takes the cracked spectacles off his nose, and folds them. She places them on the Roll.

"He did not fail to finish," she says.

"No." Zhao's voice shakes at last. "He never did."

* * *

The hardest name is the last on her own list, and she does not read it aloud.

It is near dawn. The audience has thinned. The sleepers have been carried out, the mourners have gone to their beds, and only a handful remain, huddled by the door. Zhao sits alone in the Clan Head's chair with the Roll on her knees and her husband's cold hand in hers.

She did not notice when it happened. She was reading the name of a girl who had been three years old, and when she looked down, she saw that his chest had stopped. He had gone quietly, as he did everything, with one last squeeze of her fingers, and a smile that stayed.

She sits with him a long while.

She remembers how they met. It was thirty years before she took the Seat, at a harvest feast, when she was a girl of nineteen with a bad temper and he was a quartermaster's son with a ladle and a grin. He had spilled soup on her. He had apologized for an hour. She had decided, there and then, to marry him just to stop the apologies.

She remembers the day her mother died, and his hand on her shoulder. The day she took the Seat, and his quiet voice: you'll be good at it. The nights she came to bed in a fury at the Council, and he said only tell me, and listened until the fury was gone. Sixty-three years of listening.

He kept the winter stores like a miser and the festival wine like a priest.

She has said it so often that she thinks it is the truth. But it is not the whole of it. The whole of it is that he kept her. In sixty years of storms, he was the one fixed thing, the warm place she came home to, and she did not know until now how much of herself she had rested on him.

She bends and kisses his forehead.

"You old fool," she says. "You said you'd see the spring."

The lamp gutters. In the doorway, Qinghe lifts the kettle and sets it back on its hook, quietly, so as not to wake anyone.

Zhao straightens. She wipes her eyes with the heel of her hand. She reaches for the pen that Pei An laid down, and finds it still warm. She opens the Roll to the black column, and dips the nib, and writes in her own hard upright script, below the girl named Ping, one more line.

Dao, quartermaster. Husband. Aged eighty-four. He kept the stores.

She blots it. She closes the book.

Then, for the first time in a week, the Clan Head of the Lin family puts her head down on the cover of the Roll, among her dead, and weeps.
